title: Typhoon Dujuan Forces Nearly 2 Million People to Leave Home in Japan
summary:
Imagine winds so strong they can knock you off your feet — that's what Typhoon Dujuan brought to Japan on Monday. Nearly two million people were told to leave their homes and go somewhere safe. That's like every person in a big city packing up at once.

Dujuan is a huge storm with winds blowing at 130 kilometres per hour. Some gusts reached 194 km/h — faster than a race car on a highway. The winds knocked out power for more than 50,000 people. Hundreds of flights were cancelled, and trains stopped running.

Japan's weather agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life," which means the storm was very dangerous. Later, they lowered many of the warnings, but one town called Oshima still faces danger.

This is Japan's 25th typhoon this year. The storm hit during a five-day holiday, so fun events got cancelled. The Rock in Japan music festival and the Tokyo Game Show both called off Monday's plans. Even Japan's Prime Minister, Sanae Takaichi, delayed her trip to the United States to keep an eye on the storm.

Scientists say a "super El Niño" — warm ocean water — is making these storms stronger. Warmer water gives typhoons more energy, like giving a toy car a bigger battery.
why_it_matters: Knowing what storm warnings mean can help your family stay safe, and it shows how weather far away can cancel holidays, travel and even music festivals that people look forward to.

background_read: Japan (an island country in East Asia) is hit by many typhoons every year, mostly in summer and early autumn. Typhoons are the same kind of storm that Americans call hurricanes, and they grow over warm ocean water.
The Tokyo Game Show (a huge yearly event where companies show off new video games) and the Rock in Japan music festival (a big outdoor concert) were both called off on Monday because of the storm.
Sanae Takaichi (Japan's prime minister, the country's top leader), the weather agency, and town leaders all use warnings to help people leave dangerous places before a storm arrives.
Article_Structure: WHO: Nearly two million people in Japan were told to leave home, along with Japan's weather agency, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and the organisers of the Rock in Japan music festival and the Tokyo Game Show.
WHAT: Typhoon Dujuan hit with winds of 130 km/h and gusts of 194 km/h, knocking out power for more than 50,000 people, cancelling hundreds of flights, stopping trains and calling off events.
WHERE: Japan — the storm struck on Monday, and the town of Oshima still faces danger even after many warnings were lowered.
WHY: The weather agency called it an 'imminent threat to life,' and scientists say a 'super El Niño' — warm ocean water — is making storms like this stronger.

perspectives.description: Officials and weather experts say telling two million people to leave home is the right call, because getting people out early saves lives when winds are this strong.
People on the five-day holiday lost their trips, concerts and game-show plans, so some may feel the warnings were over the top — even though the danger was real.
Researchers point out that warmer ocean water, like the 'super El Niño,' gives typhoons extra energy, which could mean stronger storms in the years ahead.
